newsitem.title: USA: Bre-X a gold mine for U.S. lawyers.
newsitem.headline: Bre-X a gold mine for U.S. lawyers.

text.p: The troubles of Canadian mining firm Bre-X Minerals Ltd have touched off a gold rush for U.S. attorneys.
At least five shareholder suits have been filed against the besieged company in U.S. courts in cities ranging from New York to San Francisco to Del Rio, Texas.
The suits allege that Bre-X executives inflated projections about the size of gold deposits at the company's Busang property in Indonesia.

The suits seek unspecified damages for a still unknown pool of shareholders who bought the stock as far back as January 17, 1994 and all the way up to March 27, when high-flying Bre-X shares took a mighty tumble.

The suits still must be certified by a federal judge as class actions, which means they would represent all shareholders who bought the stock during the period in dispute, not just the named plaintiffs.
Attorneys said they expect the case to be consolidated into one for adjudication by a single judge, although that move is likely months away.
Bre-X had reported that its Busang project on the Indonesian island of Borneo contained 71 million ounces of gold deposits, making it one of the biggest finds of the century.

Its stock soared until last week when would-be Busang partner Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc said its testing of the deposit turned up "insignificant" amounts of the valuable ore. On March 27, Bre-X's stock market value plummeted nearly C$3 billion as panic selling set in.

The lawsuits allege that the sell-off was the inevitable result of behavior by Bre-X president David Walsh and senior vice president John Felderhof who, as one of the suits charged, "undertook...to perpetrate an elaborate mining hoax."

The suits charge that, while Bre-X's stock rose, Walsh and Felderhof were getting rich by selling off shares. One of the suits, filed by the firm of Schubert and Reed in San Francisco, said the two men made "in excess of $29 million" on their stock trading.
In fact, the suits charge, Busang has very little gold, certainly not enough to make a mine economically viable.
All allegations have been denied by the Bre-X executives, who say they believe further testing of the Busang deposit will prove they were correct about how much gold it contains.
One attorney, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters the lawsuits would likely still go ahead even if big gold deposits are present.

"It will depend on how much they find. If they prove they have 71 million ounces, then the suits go forward. If they find 200 million ounces, probably not," the attorney said. The 200 million ounce threshhold comes from a statement once made by Felderhof, who said Busang's deposits could be that big.
No one knows how many more suits may be filed against Bre-X, but on Thursday its legal battles moved to another front when the first Canadian suit was filed in Windsor, Ontario.
